usage: This is the standard, everyday way to ask someone's name in the Levant. It is used in casual and semi-formal situations with peers or people younger than you. For older individuals, authority figures, or in formal settings, speakers often switch to 'shu ism 7adertak' (what is the name of your presence) to show respect.

variants.label: to a woman
variants.note: Use this when addressing a single female.

variants.label: to a group
variants.note: Use this when addressing two or more people (in Jordanian and Palestinian, 'shu ismkom' is more common).

variants.label: formal, to a man
variants.note: Use this to show respect to an older man, a customer, or in a professional setting.

variants.label: formal, to a woman
variants.note: Use this to show respect to an older woman, a customer, or in a professional setting.

examples.arabic: مَرْحَبا، أنا جْديد هون. شُو اسْمَك؟
examples.transliteration: mar7aba, ana jdid hon. shu ismak?
examples.english: Hello, I'm new here. What's your name?

examples.arabic: عَفْواً، ما سْمِعْت مْنيح، شُو اسْمِك؟
examples.english: Sorry, I didn't hear well, what's your name? (to a woman)
Welcome to you all, what are your names?
